senses.definition: Deep awareness of the suffering of others that people have to the point of them being motivated to relieve such states.
examples: Oh! the unspeakable privilege to have Him for our Father, who is the Father of mercies and compassions, and those not barren, fruitless pityings, for He is withal the God of all consolations.

quotes.text: Other people's problems, they overwhelm my mind / They say compassion is a virtue, but I don't have the time
quotes.reference: 1977, David Byrne, “No Compassion”, in Talking Heads: 77, performed by Talking Heads:

quotes.text: In many ways, people today lack compassion as a way to internalize and experience the inner soul of the other person, animals, and the universe. We need to reintroduce compassion so humanity may survive.
quotes.reference: 2002, Werner J. Krieglstein, Compassion: A New Philosophy of the Other, page 149:

quotes.text: Ethics of compassion are grounded in one's mindful commitment to one's own happiness with the recognition that the well being that one wishes for oneself also is wished for by others.
quotes.reference: 2008, Richard Reilly, Ethics of Compassion: Bridging Ethical Theory and Religious Moral Discourse, page 1:

quotes.text: From Master's words, I understand that having compassion does not mean allowing people to take advantage of us. We can be kind but we should uphold moral values.
quotes.reference: 2020 January 28, “My Understanding Of What It Means to Be Compassionate”, in Minghui:

senses.definition: (by extension, psychology) Deep awareness of the individual experiences of suffering of others or themselves that people have to the point of them being motivated to relieve such experiences, as reflected by the psychological term self-compassion.
examples: True leadership lies in compassion, not in coercion.

quotes.text: Similarly to the practice of loving kindness, meditation on compassion towards our own experience builds the foundation for expansion of the circle of compassion towards others.
quotes.reference: 2013, Dusana Dorjee, Mind, Brain and the Path to Happiness — A Guide to Buddhist Mind Training and the Neuroscience of Meditation, page 75:

quotes.text: O heavens, can you hear a good man groan / And not relent, or not compassion him?
quotes.reference: c. 1588–1593 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Lamentable Tragedy of Titus Andronicus”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London: […] Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene i], line 124:

quotes.text: Both wanted in early life the one thing essential to every individual, of whatever nature or degree of intellect, a kind, compassioning adviser; - a true friend;[…].
quotes.reference: 1830, “The Last of the Supernaturalists”, in James Fraser, editor, Fraser's Magazine, volume 1, page 226:

quotes.text: The widow's tears flowed wildly. / But Oh! a harbinger of life approached — / God, manifest in flesh — compassioned her, / And bade her weep no more.
quotes.reference: 1836, William A. Brewer, The Widow's Son, in Recreations of a Merchant; Or, The Christian Sketch-book, page 27:
